If one were to assert an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the faults of annihilationism and eternalism would ensue. For, when one examines that annihilation through such reasoning and scriptural authority (*āgama*), it cannot be established; thus, such annihilation is not tenable.
Question: Why is it not established? Answer:
Because it lacks a cause and because it does not cease.
That which is called "annihilation" is defined as the cessation into non-existence.
Being without existence and without cause, if there were no cessation, it would be like a rabbit's horn.
If a phenomenon possesses an intrinsic nature, one can speak of its cause and its cessation, just as in the case of a jar.
The Master spoke thus, as expressed in this verse:
"A phenomenon has a cause and has cessation; It can be perceived, just like a sprout."
"In cessation there is no one who ceases; therefore, there is no cause for cessation.
Because this lacks a cause, it is known to be non-existent, and furthermore, because it does not cease.
Your mind being thus, and desiring to seek the truth, you should not cling to annihilation.
He asked:
"I have now understood; I shall accept this non-annihilation."
If this abandonment is included, it is the most base and evil among all evils.
Why is it not eternal?
The answer is:
How could I not have previously stated that there is no arising?
If there is no arising, how can there be permanence?
If that which does not arise were permanent, then even a rabbit’s horn would be permanent.
This is not possible; therefore, it is not permanent.
The World-Honored One has said:
"If a dharma does not arise, one cannot say it is permanent, nor is it subject to annihilation."
Therefore, both permanence and annihilation are untenable, as they fall into extremes.
If you think that space, the self, and so forth exist without being produced, and thus are permanent, [that too is incorrect].
As for the claim that, according to what has been said, there exists a phenomenon that lacks causes and conditions yet is truly eternal—
and on this basis, that the self and so forth are established as eternal—
this argument is not tenable; why bother with such deliberation?
The son of a barren woman may be black or white, yet he is as non-existent as space;
your contemplation that this [self] is eternal is likewise so.
It is asked:
Regarding those things such as space, how can they be non-existent?
The answer is:
in space and so forth, no entity can ultimately be found; it is just like a rabbit’s horn, which is ultimately non-existent in this way.
Each of the six sense faculties cannot perceive them individually; likewise, emptiness and so forth are also unattainable. Therefore, one knows they do not exist.
Because they do not exist, the argument that space and so forth are eternal is untenable.
Furthermore, because it does not arise, the absence of meaning is established.

According to your view, regarding that which is a "existent dharma" (*bhāva*), if it has not yet come to be, neither the non-existent dharma nor the existent dharma is established; this is because it does not arise and lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If there were an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it would exist by virtue of its own essence;
because it exists, it would not require combination, for it already exists.
If there is no intrinsic nature, then within the absence of intrinsic nature there is no phenomenon (*dharma*), because it is a non-entity, just like a rabbit's horn.
As it is said in verse:
"Because entities lack intrinsic nature, therefore no phenomena exist.
That 'this arises from those conditions'— this meaning is not so."
If you think that space exists because it possesses characteristics,
those characteristics themselves do not exist, for they have no beginning, no end, and no duality.
Furthermore, there is that which is unarisen. If an unarisen dharma possessed characteristics, then rabbit horns should likewise possess characteristics such as length or shortness;
however, this is not the case.
If you think that my characteristic can be apprehended, [we reply that] because those characteristics are not grasped by the six consciousnesses, the characteristic cannot be apprehended.
If you think that what manifests as a characteristic is perceived directly, then you lose your own doctrine, because it would be apprehended by the sense faculties.
If this were so, then the "self" (ātman) you have established would be impermanent and so forth.
If you think that what is not an object of the sense faculties is not included within the characteristics [of the aggregates],
it is asked:
although it has been refuted in this way, the self (ātman) truly exists, because it is mentioned in a single phrase.
If this were expressed by taking two characters as a single phrase, one would know that "it exists," just as in the case of a ritual water vessel (*śīkara*).
Since I likewise express it by taking two characters as a single phrase, one knows that there is a self; thus, this single character "I" (*ātman*) corresponds to those two characters.
Answer: This statement is not established, because it is a one-sided argument.
It is like that space, and also like a dream; here, the single character "dream" (夢) reverses those two characters [of the previous argument].
I am also like this; therefore, there is no self.
Just as that space is, and also like a dream—all these things described by two syllables are entirely non-existent.
I am also like this; therefore, there is no self.
Furthermore, there is no self because it is something produced.
If a thing is produced, one knows that it is without self, just like that jar.
Since this body is produced through such activity, the body is without self, because it is a product of activity.

If you think that there is a self because you perceive signs such as life-force within the body, then since those signs of life-force and so forth are impermanent, any deliberation on them as being permanent cannot be established.

If you think that I do not actually say that there is a phenomenon which is eternal, nor do I say that non-existence constitutes annihilation, but rather that there is another phenomenon which functions throughout the three periods of time and is called "eternal" because it does not perish—[that is not so].
If there were no dharmas, there could be no meaning; therefore, I say that dharmas are eternal.
If there were no dharmas, it would constitute annihilation.
This is my intention, which I shall now explain.
If there were such a thing as a dharma, it could be said to undergo transmigration through the three periods of time.
However, a permanent dharma is fixedly established, immovable and unchanging; how, then, could it undergo transmigration through the three periods of time?
If it is subject to transmigration, then it is impermanent.
Question: In what way is it impermanent?
Answer: If it were past, how could it be permanent?
If it were past, it would be impermanent.
What is the past?
The past is called lost, exhausted, ceased, and non-existent in essence. How could that be permanent?
If it lacks essence, how can it be the past?
If there were a substantial entity, how could it be past?
If it existed [as a substance], then even the son of a barren woman would have to be permanent, because he lacks substantiality.
Furthermore, if it is past, the meaning of permanence cannot be established.
The doctrine that the future world is eternal is likewise not established.
Question: Why is it not established?
The answer is:
This "future" is called non-existent, called unarisen, and called unmanifested.
If it is thus, how could it be permanent?
If it were permanent, then even a rabbit's horn would be permanent; this principle is untenable.
If you claim that there is a thing, how can it be both permanent and yet future? Or how can it be merely future?
The meaning is inconsistent.
Furthermore, the meaning of "eternal in the present" is also not established.
Question:
Why is it not established?
The answer is:
this "present" is called the present because it manifests as the flow of dharmas.
Those presently existing phenomena do not abide for even a single thought-moment.
If they were to abide for a single thought-moment, they would abide for an entire eon;
yet this characteristic of abiding is, in reality, unattainable.
Because there is no abiding, even mindfulness is non-existent.
If mindfulness were to undergo transformation, how could it be permanent?
If it does not arise, how could there be the establishment of the temporal periods of the present, future, and past?
Because time has no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If it did have an intrinsic nature, then the past, future, and present would not be time;
yet if they were time, then the past, future, and present would lack intrinsic nature.
At that time, whether [time] is identical to or different from its substance, neither position is logically tenable.
Furthermore, since the very existence of time and its substance cannot be established, how much less could it be past, future, present, or eternal?
If an entity were permanent, its very existence as an entity would be unestablished.
Since its existence as an entity is unestablished, how could it be established as permanent?
Therefore, permanence does not exist.
As for your thought that what is non-existent is not a dharma,
this is most certainly unestablished.
For what reason do you claim that what is non-existent is not a dharma?
If that which is non-existent is not the Dharma, then that which is existent is likewise not the Dharma, because non-existence and existence are mutually opposed.
Since there is no non-existent Dharma, the existent Dharma is also non-existent, because that non-existent Dharma is not established.
If non-existent dharmas do not constitute existent dharmas, how can there be existent dharmas that constitute existent dharmas?
How can there be existent dharmas that are called "existent dharmas"?
If you think that these existent dharmas further possess causes and conditions by which they exist as existent dharmas; [then...]
Then, this existent dharma and that non-existent dharma would not be in opposition;
this is now explained.

If you conceptually differentiate this existent dharma as having yet another existent dharma, then these two existents would be equal and similar in their mutual correspondence, unlike the case of the non-existent.
Does this existent phenomenon (dharma) further possess an existent phenomenon, or does it not?
I shall now explain this.
If that existent phenomenon further possessed an existent phenomenon, there would be an infinite regress.
If you think that an existent dharma arises from a non-existent dharma, then this would mean that a dharma arises without a cause;
in that case, the meaning of "existent dharma" is not established.
Thus, while there is no phenomenon, a phenomenon arises; yet there is no one who possesses faith and delight.
Regarding such existence and non-existence, you should abandon them and not grasp at them.
Furthermore, there is the clear illumination of phenomena through their mutual contrast, which clearly demonstrates those existing phenomena.
If it possesses an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), one may say that it is an existent phenomenon (*dharma*).
If it lacks an intrinsic nature, then it cannot be called an existent phenomenon, for its nature is not established.
If its nature is not established, how can existence or non-existence be established?
You should abandon this conceptualization of existence and non-existence;
what use is it to you?
Furthermore, there is another interpretation regarding such phenomena as cessation and arising, annihilation and permanence, and so forth.
What is the meaning of this?
Does it exist within a single entity simultaneously,
or does it occur sequentially?
I shall now explain this.
How can non-associated dharmas be in a single location?
Because they are mutually contradictory.
Since cessation and so forth are mutually contradictory, they cannot coexist in the same location.
How could they not destroy one another within a single entity?
If you intend to claim that within a single moment there is both cessation and arising, as well as annihilation and permanence, then this is inconsistent.
If you further claim that within a single entity, it does not transform in a single moment, but rather transforms with distinctions across various different moments, then this is inconsistent.
Question: In what sense is it called "inconsistent"?
The answer is:

If it were thus, then one dharma would arise from something entirely different, another dharma would cease from something entirely different, one dharma would be severed from something entirely different, and another dharma would be eternal through something entirely different.
Because of such [consequences], how could there be any distinction within this single entity?

If you intend to avoid such faults by asserting that the destruction of one thing is distinct from the thing itself, and that there is a separate arising, a separate cessation, and a separate change occurring outside of the thing—such a position is untenable.
Question: In what way is it not established? Answer:
If it were so, then one could say that even a single entity both exists and does not exist; such a principle is impossible.
Therefore, the meanings of "identity" and "difference" are not established.

Not only do identity and difference fail to be established for cessation and so forth, but furthermore, for which phenomena—if they possess cessation and so forth—do identity and difference with that cessation and so forth fail to be established?
Question: In what sense do identity and difference fail to be established for cessation and so forth alone?
Is it because identity and difference cannot be established for all phenomena?
The answer is:
All phenomena are likewise such that identity and difference cannot be established.
As the verse says:
"It is neither of one meaning nor of different meanings. Question:
Why is it that the identity or difference of all phenomena cannot be established?
The answer is:
because they are unarisen, like the son of a barren woman.
If phenomena were to arise, the concepts of identity and difference would be established.
However, if all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen, how can the concepts of identity and difference be established?
They are like the son of a barren woman; being inherently unarisen, they lack intrinsic nature.
Furthermore, there is no intrinsic nature because of causes and conditions.
As for the dharma of causes and conditions, no dharma can be apprehended.
If it is a matter of causes and conditions, then it is not "arising," as stated in the sūtras.
This principle of identity and difference is not established.
Question: In what sense are causes and conditions said to be "non-arising"?
If there is no arising, how can it be called "causal condition"?
If it is a causal condition, how can there be no arising?
If there is no arising, how can there be a causal condition?
If it is called "non-arising" based on its causes and conditions, this meaning is inconsistent.
The answer is:
this is indeed inconsistent.
If one speaks of causes and conditions, it is inconsistent.
If the essence [of a thing] already exists, how can there be causes and conditions, since it already exists?
If it does not exist, then it is a non-entity; how can there be causes and conditions for that which is a non-entity?
If non-existent dharmas possess causes and conditions, then even the horns of a rabbit must likewise possess causes and conditions.
Since the cause has no substance—because it is a non-entity—it is like a flower in the sky.
Therefore, this principle is established:
when one contemplates causes and conditions, they are found to be non-arising.
What are these causes and conditions?
Question:
There are two kinds of causes and conditions:
first, internal; second, external.
The internal refers to what is known as ignorance conditioned by formations, up to old age and death;
the external dependent origination refers to seeds, sprouts, and so forth within the entire vessel-world (bhājana-loka).
The answer is:
We shall now deliberate upon this Dharma as follows.
If you were to analyze these twelve factors of dependent origination, such as ignorance and so forth, according to what you have said, these twelve factors would be like the parts of a chariot.
Regarding the parts of a chariot, they are called "causes and conditions" (hetu-pratyaya). Because these twelve factors come together in harmony, they are called "causes and conditions.
Is each individual part itself a cause and condition?
Are these two [categories] each further divided into two based on causes and conditions?
Or is there yet another set of causes and conditions beyond all these external factors?
Or are they merely appearances?
When all these phenomena are thus examined, none are found to be consistent.
Question: In what sense are they said to be inconsistent?
Answer: Because of the nature of moment-to-moment arising.
If it were merely a single entity, there would be no causes and conditions.
Question:
Why is it that a single [entity] lacks causes and conditions? Answer:
If this were the case, then only ignorance would function as a causal condition, while the others would not.

Furthermore, even these two would not constitute a causal condition, because cessation and arising do not coexist; just as arising and non-arising are not in conjunction, so too are they incompatible.
The analysis of the parts of a chariot is likewise inconsistent, because the causal conditions for their conjunction cannot be established.
We observe that the parts of a chariot exist in conjunction as phenomena at one and the same time.
When ignorance and its factors are present, no dharma is perceived at that time.
By such causes and conditions, it is called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*),
just as one speaks of a "chariot" based on the parts of a chariot.
If ignorance were of equal status [with the factors], it would not be thus; for as birth and cessation arise and perish, phenomena lack any combination.
If there is no combination, what phenomenon could be taught?
If there is nothing that is spoken, how can one speak of the Dharma?
All verbal expressions are the characteristics (*nimitta*) of dharmas.
How could these characteristics be said to exist?
As the Ācārya Deva said in verse:
"A single dharma is called 'without essence,' because there is no combination.
If even one thing lacks essence, then there is no combination."
If there were a separate dharma existing apart from the various parts, it would not be a causal condition, because it would not arise.
Thus, the meaning that causal conditions do not produce [anything] is established.
As the Buddha said:
"To speak of causes and conditions, causes and conditions are themselves empty.
Therefore, one should relinquish the notion of causes and conditions and not grasp at them.
When one reflects in this way, both the identity and the difference of things are neither established."
Furthermore, having perceived "one," one grasps it in relation to its opposite, "the other";
and because one has already perceived "the other," one grasps it in relation to its opposite, "the one.
Since these opposites are not established, as the verse says:
Apart from various causes and conditions, no further phenomena arise;
nor can any phenomenon be found apart from non-different causes and conditions.
Apart from the various, there is nothing further that is different; yet apart from the non-different, difference also does not exist.
"If there were no difference, then difference could not be apprehended.
Thus, one should relinquish both identity and difference rather than grasping them.
Having thus relinquished them, one knows that their intrinsic nature is empty.
The mind contemplates that emptiness; what use is there in grasping at what is false and unreal?
It is asked: "So it is, so it is."
The intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty by its very essence; this is the ultimate truth, which is true and real.
Only now do I understand that the Tathāgata speaks words of truth.
As the World-Honored One has said, the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is empty by its very essence, because they lack self-nature.
Furthermore, why is it that for all people in the world, the past and future are not established as being directly perceived?
The answer is:
because of the *āgama*.
Question: What is the Āgama? Answer:
Regarding this meaning, the Tathāgata spoke thus in the *Mahāsūtra*:
"Subhūti, all dharmas are empty in their coming, going, and movement."
That person does not realize this, grasping and clinging to it without relinquishing it.
Yet these dharmas of emptiness neither go nor come; there is not a single dharma that is not empty.
Furthermore, he also said: “All dharmas do not come.”
This is established both by scripture (*āgama*) and by reasoning (*yukti*).
If a phenomenon is unarisen, it has no coming or going, just like a rabbit's horn.
Thus, this meaning is proven.
Furthermore, a verse says:
"That which has already gone does not go; that which has not yet gone also does not go.
Apart from that which has already gone and that which has not yet gone, the presently going is not going."
This is further explained in detail:
What is "going"? What phenomenon is "going"?
Who is it that goes?
If it is "I" who goes, since there is no self (*ātman*), the meaning of going is not established.
According to your doctrine, the self is eternal, immovable, and unshakable; how then could it go?
If I were able to go, then empty space would also go; yet this empty space truly has no quality of going.
This "self" cannot go from this direction to that direction; it neither departs nor joins.
The "self" (ātman) that you have established as being omnipresent has no place to go, because it is sovereign and pervasive throughout all things.
For this reason, the self does not go.
If you think that because the body follows the mind, there is therefore "volitional formation" (*saṃskāra*),
this argument is not tenable.
This is because it entails the fallacies of being both permanent and impermanent, the fallacies of having parts and lacking parts, and the fallacies of being both material and immaterial.
Because the mind is not something created, the body does not follow its movements, and such movement cannot be apprehended.
Since the existence or non-existence of the mind and body is not established as permanent, how could it move from this place to that place?
As the disciples of Kāpila maintain: the transmigrating person (puruṣa) proceeds by means of superior causes and conditions;
this is called "going" (gati). Having acted, the person returns; this is called "returning" (āgati). Thus, it is through these superior factors that going and coming exist.
This is my explanation: you are now making a pill of joy out of flowers in the sky and giving it to the son of a barren woman to eat.
That which is superior does not exist, yet you think that by the power of that superiority, a person comes and goes.
Although the Victorious One (Jina) is eternal, he is able to cause a person to come and go; the principle is likewise so.
As you understand it, just as when a person walks, it is not an act of creation, nor does it accomplish any traversed phenomenon, such as a village or a city.
This has already been refuted previously because [conditioned phenomena] do not arise.
Furthermore, as for those who claim that conditioned things exist, they have no going, because they lack movement.
Motion is a characteristic; such a characteristic is not the essence of the conditioned.
Thus it is taught that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent from moment to moment; since they do not abide in this way, how could there be "action"?
Therefore, the verse says:
"That which has arisen may be called 'action,' and it may also be called the 'agent'."
Thus, it should be known that although conditioned phenomena arise and proceed, such arising has already been refuted previously.
Furthermore, there is a verse that says:
"Conditioned things have no place from which they come, For they do not abide for even a single moment."
Furthermore, there is no place to which it goes; for this reason, there is no abiding.
Thus, it is illogical for conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) to travel to another location, because they lack the activity of motion.
In this way, since even the existence of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) is not established, how much less could there be the movement of a conditioned thing, or its arrival and subsequent return?
This is because their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is empty.
If you should think that the aggregates (*skandha*) possess movement and are therefore not subsumed under the category of the conditioned; [that would be incorrect].
This interpretation is incorrect, because the aggregates (skandhas) are not established.
Question: In what way are they not established?
Answer: Because causes and conditions are empty.
What is the meaning of this?
Just as the horns of a rabbit ultimately lack any causes or conditions, so too it is with the aggregates such as form; their causes and conditions are ultimately unobtainable.
Knowing it thus, because causes and conditions are empty, the aggregates such as form do not exist.
As the Ācārya has said in verse:
"Separated from the causes and conditions of form, Form cannot be apprehended."
Nor is it apart from form that one perceives the causes and conditions of form;
yet apart from the causes and conditions of form, form itself accomplishes form.
An entity cannot obtain causes and conditions, nor can it exist without causes and conditions.
One should understand it thus: because there are no causes and conditions, form is non-existent.
This applies to all things alike; even if you should think that atoms exist, [they too are non-existent].
Since this is not established, the meaning of such movement cannot be established.
As you have stated— that all presently perceived things possess the movement of coming and going—
this is not the case, because such perception is not established.
Question: Why is it not established? Answer:
This manifest [object] is called either cognition or a thing.
I shall now explain this.
If it is cognition, one must state what that cognition is.
Whose manifestation is this?
If the six objects of perception were obtainable, then since objects do not exist, how could it be known that this is a manifestation?

For one who possesses the realization of moment-to-moment cessation, there is no manifestation; even to the point of having no doubt as to whether manifestation exists or does not exist—this is supreme.
The cognition that cognizes the manifest is itself not manifest, because it cognizes an object.

Since cognition is not established [as manifest], if one asserts the existence of a "substantial person" (pudgala), one abandons one's own doctrine; for how could such a manifest phenomenon appear as a substantial entity?
In the *Pramāṇaviniścaya*, this matter is extensively refuted.
What is this that appears?
What is it that appears now?
Furthermore, the Tathāgata has spoken this verse:
"The eye does not see forms, And consciousness does not know phenomena;
This is the foremost secret, Which the world cannot understand."
Regarding this meaning, the Ācārya said:
"No one has ever been able to see themselves by themselves;
if one cannot see oneself, how can one see another?"
Thus, there is no manifestation, and manifestation cannot be apprehended.
As for what you say— that all that is manifestly perceived has coming and going—
this meaning is not so.
Since the past and future are not form, how can they be said to be manifest?
Since they are not obtained by the eye nor conceived by the mind, they do not constitute existence; how then could they be seen as manifest?
If you think that existence is known through inference because there is inference, then inference itself is not established, because it presupposes prior perception;
for both inference and perception are unestablished.
Inference is known as "knowledge," which is a conceptualization of the mind.
Such inference can only be apprehended by the mind, because it is subsumed within the mind.
Therefore, this [proposed] meaning is not so, for the mind itself does not exist.
Question:
Regarding this principle, if phenomena are unarisen, then there is neither coming nor going, nor even a present.
What person of settled mind and sound intellect would accept this doctrine—that within all unarisen phenomena there is coming and going?

Thus, whether it be the meaning of difference, the meaning of identity, the meaning of permanence, the meaning of annihilation, the meaning of arising, or the meaning of cessation—all these are entirely unestablished because of non-arising.
Furthermore, how is it that all phenomena are unarisen?
The answer is given in verse:
"Neither from self nor from another, Neither from both nor without cause— All phenomena are thus; Therefore, they are all unarisen.
*The Exposition of the Meaning of the Madhyamaka-śāstra Entering the First Chapter of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, Part II.
